title: Maimonides' code
hookLine: the Mishneh Torah sets out Jewish law in one voice, without citing sources

lines: ALL OF THE LAW, IN ORDER.
cards: No footnotes. For some readers that was the problem with this book, and for its author it was the point.

Moses ben Maimon, called Maimonides in English and Rambam in Hebrew, set out to write down Jewish law in one orderly work, not only the laws people kept in his day, but the laws of the Temple and of kings too.
And he wrote it as plain statements. This is required. This is forbidden.
This is how it is done. No rabbi says, no trail back to the page it came from. After weeks of a Talmud full of voices, here is a book with one.

teach.b: Its name is Mishneh Torah, often rendered a repetition of the Torah. Turn it four ways. First, the voice.
Where the Talmud keeps every side of an argument, Maimonides gives the ruling and moves on.
In his introduction he explains why: a person could read the written Torah first, then this book, and know the oral law without needing another book in between.

Second, where it begins: not with blessings or with Shabbat, but with God. The opening law, in the section on the foundations of the Torah, is to know that there is a First Being who brought all things into existence.
Study, character and repentance sit in the same work as the laws of damages and of the Sabbath. For Maimonides, belief and behavior belong in one book. Third, who it was for.
He wrote in clear, orderly Hebrew rather than the Talmud's Aramaic, and arranged everything by topic, so a learner could find a law without knowing where in the Talmud it lived.
Rabbi Abraham ben David of Posquières, known as the Rabad, wrote sharp critical notes on the code.
Some worried that with no sources, nobody could check a ruling or follow its reasoning, and that people might stop learning the Talmud itself.
And the twist: open a printed Mishneh Torah today and the Rabad's notes are there on the page, along with later commentaries that went back and traced each ruling to its source.
The book without footnotes ended up surrounded by them.

how: Students learn the Mishneh Torah alone or in classes, and some follow a daily study cycle through it. Printed editions surround the text with commentaries that trace each ruling back to its sources.

games.q: you're Maimonides. you want anyone to be able to know Jewish law without wading through the whole Talmud. how do you write it?
o: copy out the Talmud's debates in order.
state each ruling plainly, by topic, with no sources.
write down only the laws people keep today.
games.why: he states the rulings plainly, arranged by topic, in clear Hebrew. later commentaries went back and supplied the sources he left out.

practice: Choose something you know well, how to make a family dish, or how to get from your door to the nearest grocery store, and say it to yourself in plain steps: first this, then this, no "well, it depends."
Notice how much you have to understand before you can say something simply.
